summary: This Best Current Practice describes how the IAB sets up and maintains liaison relationships between the IETF and other standards bodies, consortia and industry forums. It also covers appointing liaison managers and representatives and what is expected of them.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF sometimes needs to talk with other groups making standards. This document explains how it picks who does the talking and how those relationships are managed.

questions: how does the iab manage liaison relationships
what is an ietf liaison manager
subtitle: How the IAB sets up liaisons with other standards bodies, appoints liaison managers, and approves liaison statements.

tldr.problem: The IETF often has to coordinate with other standards bodies, consortia and industry forums to avoid overlapping work, and needs a clear way to manage those relationships.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB creates liaison relationships when they are mutually agreeable, appoints an IETF liaison manager (and sometimes more representatives), and requires named IETF leaders to approve any formal liaison statement.
tldr.outcome: This is a Best Current Practice (BCP 102). It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 4052 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 102), and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Liaison Relationships and Personnel
sections.content:
The IETF is one of several Standards Development Organizations (SDOs), and needs to communicate and coordinate with other organizations to avoid overlapping work and to manage interactions between groups. When this effort is formalized, the result is called a liaison relationship.

A person from the IETF is designated as the IETF liaison manager for each relationship. If the relationship is complex or broad, more people may be designated to handle parts of the communications, coordinated by the liaison manager. The other organization will often designate its own liaison manager to the IETF, but managing those people is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When two clubs want to work together, each picks a person to be the messenger so nothing gets lost.

sections.title: Why the IAB Handles Liaisons
sections.content:
The IETF has chartered the Internet Architecture Board to manage liaison relationships. Under its charter (RFC 2850), the IAB represents the interests of the IETF and the Internet Society in technical liaison relationships. Liaison relationships are kept as informal as possible and must be of demonstrable value to the IETF's technical mandate. The IAB appoints individual IETF participants as liaison managers or representatives.

A relationship is most valuable where there are areas of technical development of mutual interest. It can prevent inadvertent duplication of effort without obstructing either organization, and provide authoritative information on one organization's dependencies on the other's work.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB is the group that decides who the IETF's messengers are, and it only sets up a link when it is really useful.

sections.title: Setting Up a Relationship
sections.content:
A relationship is set up when it is mutually agreeable and needed for a specific purpose, in the view of the other organization, the IAB and the IETF participants doing the work. There is no set process or form. The IETF participants and the peer organization approach the IAB and, after discussion, agree to form it. Sometimes the scope and guidelines are documented, as in RFC 3113, RFC 3131 and RFC 3356.

New standardization work that results for the IETF is undertaken under the usual IETF procedures (RFC 2026). The IAB expects each side to use the relationship carefully, allow time for processes in the other organization, and not make unreasonable demands.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no form to fill in. People just ask the IAB, they talk it over, and everyone agrees to be polite and patient.

sections.title: Liaison Managers and Representatives
sections.content:
Most work happens in the usual way within each organization, so most communication is informal, such as working group or mailing list discussions. The liaison manager makes sure communication is maintained, productive and timely, and helps redirect a message sent to the wrong party, for example to the wrong working group or without copying the Area Director.

Liaison managers should also coordinate with other liaison managers when technical activities overlap. Anyone with a problem with a relationship should first consult the IAB's designated liaison manager and, failing a satisfactory outcome, the IAB itself.

Other liaison representatives may be named, for example for different parts of a large peer organization or to attend a particular meeting. The IAB selects them, they work closely with the liaison manager, and their responsibilities are identified when they are appointed.
sections.plainLanguage: The main messenger keeps the chat going and points letters to the right desk. Extra helpers can be added for big jobs or a single meeting.

sections.title: What a Liaison Manager Does
sections.content:
Expectations vary with the peer organization and the joint work, but generally a liaison manager appointed by the IAB is expected to:

  • Attend relevant meetings of the peer organization as needed and report material updates back to the appropriate IETF body.
  • Carry messages from the IETF when specifically instructed. These "represent the IETF", so due care and consensus must be applied.
  • Prepare occasional updates, with the target (the IAB, an AD or a WG) generally identified at appointment.
  • Oversee delivery of liaison statements addressed to the IETF and make sure timely responses are created and sent.
  • Work with the other organization so the IETF's statements are directed properly and answered promptly.
  • Coordinate with other IETF liaison managers and representatives where activities overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: The messenger goes to meetings, reports back, delivers letters, and makes sure letters get answered.

sections.title: Liaison Statements and Their Approval
sections.content:
The IETF prefers informal channels, which have historically worked well. Sometimes a more formal communication is appropriate, either alongside or instead. Many organizations use a form known as a liaison statement, and procedures for sending, managing and responding to them are discussed in a separate document.

Anyone claiming to speak for the IETF must truly represent its views, so appropriate leadership must review outgoing statements. All outgoing liaison statements are copied to the IETF Secretariat. Who must agree depends on who the statement speaks for: working group chairs for a WG, the Area Director(s) for an Area, the IETF Chair for the IETF as a whole, and the IAB Chair for the IAB. If the authority did not agree in advance and in fact disagrees, they work with the liaison manager to follow up, including a revised statement if needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Before anyone sends an official letter in the IETF's name, the right boss has to agree, and the Secretariat gets a copy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document's security section is one sentence: the security of the Internet is not threatened by these procedures. It defines administrative processes and no protocol, so it describes no further security mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: This is just about who talks to whom, so it does not put the internet at risk.
